最高人民法院

知识产权案件年度报告（续）

（2009）

（接上期）

25. 应承担民事责任的虚假宣传行为的基本条件

在前述"携程"判决案中，最高人民法院还明确了应承担民事责任的虚假宣传行为的基本条件，即应当具备经营者之间具有竞争关系、有关宣传内容足以造成相关公众误解、对经营者造成了直接损害这三个基本条件；其中对于引人误解和直接损害的后果问题，不能简单地以相关公众可能产生的误导性后果来替代原告对自身受到损害的证明责任。

最高人民法院审理认为，反不正当竞争法第九条第一款规定的引人误解的虚假宣传行为，并非都是经营者可以主张民事权利的行为。当事人可以主张民事权利的虚假宣传行为，应当符合经营者之间具有竞争关系、有关宣传内容足以造成相关公众误解、对经营者造成了直接损害这三个基本条件。对于引人误解和直接损害的后果问题，本案黄金假日公司指控的是携程计算机公司和携程商务公司的有关宣传行为构成所谓的市场混淆行为，即消费者会对携程计算机公司和携程商务公司之间在提供相关服务的主体身份及其经营资质上发生混淆或者误认。对此，携程计算机公司和携程商务公司在经营中对各自的身份表示确有不当之处，有混同使用或者模糊称谓其经营主体身份的行为，如大量使用"携程"和"携程旅行网"的简称，有关的宣传容易使人产生对市场上的"携程"是否是一家、"携程"到底是指谁、"携程旅行网"到底是谁在经营等疑问和困惑，可能会造成相关公众对二者间身份的混淆或者误认。即使是在本案审理过程中，被上诉人提交的有关诉讼文书中也有使用"携程"的简称，让人难以区分到底是指代携程计算机公司还是携程商务公司。但是，不论相关公众是否会对该二被上诉人之间主体身份及其经营资质上发生混淆或者误认，黄金假日公司并未举证证明该携程计算机公司和携程商务公司的有关行为包括上述误导性后果使黄金假日公司自身受到了直接的损害，不能简单地以相关公众可能产生上述与黄金假日公司无关的误导性后果来替代黄金假日公司对自身受到损害的证明责任。

26. 商业诋毁行为的构成条件

反不正当竞争法第十四条对商业诋毁行为做了规定，即经营者不得捏造、散布虚伪事实，损害竞争对手的商业信誉、商品声誉。

在申请再审人上海百兰王贸易发展有限公司（以下简称百兰王公司）与被申请人上海大鹤蛋品有限公司（以下简称大鹤蛋品公司）商业诋毁纠纷案〔（2009）民申字第508号〕中，最高人民法院进一步明确了商业诋毁行为的构成条件。最高人民法院在裁定中认为，反不正当竞争法调整的商业诋毁行为并不要求行为人必须直接指明诋毁的具体对象的名称，但商业诋毁指向的对象应当是可辨别的；反不正当竞争法没有对商业诋毁的语言作出限制，诋毁语言并不一定要求有感情色彩。

该案的基本案情是：上海市场上销售"蘭王"品牌鸡蛋的只有大鹤蛋品公司和百兰王公司两家公司。百兰王公司正在申请注册"蘭王"商标，但尚未获得授权。2007年3月之前，大鹤蛋品公司与百兰王公司之间就"蘭王"品牌鸡蛋在中国的生产、销售存在合作关系。双方合作终止后，百兰王公司委托案外人生产"蘭王"鸡蛋。2007年5月11日，百兰王公司在上海的日文报刊上发布了日文《声明》，包括《关于"蘭王"类似商品、假冒商品的注意公告》、《关于"蘭王"商标》和《"蘭王"蛋品的确认》，声称最近在上海市场上发现其他公司销售的与百兰王公司商品相类似的或同名的商品，该商品与百兰王公司没有任何关系，百兰王公司也无法保证该类商品的使用期限及品质；为了防患于未然，对于未经百兰王公司的允许，在市场上销售标注百兰王公司商标或相类似商标的商品的行为，百兰王公司一律认定为侵犯百兰王公司的商标权。2007年6月1日，百兰王公司发布了《相关情况》，并将其放置于百兰王公司销售的鸡蛋产品包装盒内，《相关情况》内容包括："本公司委托上海蛋品监督机构上海蛋品协会进行了调查，结果是大鹤蛋品公司根本没有鸡蛋生产的养殖场"、"一段时期内，本公司曾把GP工作委托给大鹤蛋品公司，但其在鸡蛋的管理、清洗、选定及包装方面发生了诸多问题"、"本公司认定该公司上市的相类似的商品属于以不正当竞争及获取不正当利益为目的的行为"等。大鹤蛋品公司以百兰王公司为被告提起诉讼，上海市第二中级人民法院一审认定百兰王公司的行为构成商业诋毁，判决百兰王公司立即停止不正当竞争行为、消除影响并赔偿损失。百兰王公司不服，提出上诉。上海市高级人民法院二审判决予以维持。百兰王公司不服二审判决，以其发表的《声明》没有指名道姓，其发表的《声明》和《相关情况》中的内容均是以描述事实为主、未使用诋毁性语言和骂人的话等理由，向最高人民法院申请再审。最高人民法院于2009年8月4日裁定驳回百兰王公司的再审申请。

最高人民法院审查认为，反不正当竞争法第十四条调整的商业诋毁行为并不要求行为人必须直接指明诋毁的具体对象的名称，即并不要求诋毁行为人指名道姓，但商业诋毁指向的对象应当是可辨别的。本案中，申请再审人发表的《声明》虽然没有指明针对的对象是被申请人，但当时上海仅仅有其与被申请人两家公司销售"蘭王"品牌鸡蛋，百兰王公司对此是明知的，而消费者完全可以根据该声明得出这样的判断，其他"蘭王"牌鸡蛋的经营者侵犯了百兰王公司的商标权。大鹤蛋品公司作为"蘭王"牌鸡蛋的生产者，其商业信誉和商品声誉自然会因此受到损害。因此，百兰王公司发表的《声明》构成对大鹤蛋品公司的商业诋毁。反不正当竞争法并没有对商业诋毁的语言作出限制，诋毁语言并不一律要求有感情色彩，无论是包含诸如憎恨、羞辱、藐视的语言或者说是骂人的话，还是不带任何感情色彩的陈述，只要其中涉及的事实是虚伪的，是无中生有的，并因此损害了他人的商业信誉和商品声誉，就构成商业诋毁。

五、知识产权合同案件审判

27. 技术转让合同与以技术入股的合作经营合同的区分与判断

在合同案件的审理中，确定合同的性质是审理案件的基础。由于实践中合同的复杂性，区分技术转让合同和以技术入股的合作经营合同存在一定难度。为此，应全面考虑、综合分析合同的有关约定以及当事人的履约行为，正确确定当事人所争议的合同条款的真实含义。

在申请再审人闫春梅与被申请人朱国庆技术转让合同纠纷案〔（2009）民申字第159号〕中，最高人民法院适用合同法第一百二十五条第一款的规定，按照合同所使用的词句、合同的有关条款、合同的目的、交易习惯以及诚实信用原则，确定了当事人所争议的合同条款的真实意思，从而正确认定了涉案合同的性质为预付前期技术转让费加利润提成方式的技术转让合同。

该案的基本案情是：闫春梅与朱国庆于2003年10月29日签订了一份名称为《合作经营合同》的合同，季新华作为中介人在该合同尾部签字。该合同第1条和第2条约定，闫春梅将其自主开发的VJ绿色奶牛精饲料技术独家转让给朱国庆，朱国庆以其所在地先期投入资金，设立奶牛精饲料公司并办理相关审批手续。该合同第4条"技术转让费的支付"约定，朱国庆分三期支付给闫春梅技术转让费100万元，第一期20万元将在本合同签字生效后即付；第二期20万元于生产设备安装完毕，生产出产品符合国家和企业标准后支付；第三期60万元在生产设备安装完毕后，生产出合格产品，首先从实现的利润中支付，60万元付款结束后，在一个月时间内，完成技术转让。该合同第5条"公司的股份确认"约定：该公司所有资产为朱国庆投入，原始资产与闫春梅无关，朱国庆具有全面管理决策权，并占有该公司65%的股份，闫春梅占有25%的股份，中介人占有10%股份。闫春梅股份是技术股，上述公司各股份按各自所占比例，具有获得公司利润和承担公司风险的权利和义务。合同第6条"双方行为的约定"约定：因为双方约定现有企业资金的投入和新增资产由朱国庆出资或由朱国庆利润支出，企业资产包括固定资产以及新增资产的产权与闫春梅无关。合同签订后，朱国庆即交付20万元的技术转让费。2003年11月27日，朱国庆等7人设立天翔公司（后名称变更为天祥公司），闫春梅和季新华均不是该公司股东，季新华未对此提出异议。闫春梅派其丈夫为天祥公司购买了生产设备，朱国庆安装了设备，但至诉讼中未进行调试和生产。双方认可，合同约定的技术配方的核心是菌种，闫春梅并未将菌种交付给朱国庆。2007年4月6日，朱国庆以闫春梅为被告提起诉讼，请求判令终止履行合同、闫春梅返还其技术转让费20万元并赔偿损失10万元。闫春梅以朱国庆违约为由反诉请求判令朱国庆给付其违约金30万元。江苏省淮安市中级人民法院一审认为，双方之间的技术转让合同有效，闫春梅不履行交付技术的主要合同义务，无法作价入股，朱国庆未设立合同约定的公司并不构成违约，故判决解除合同、闫春梅返还朱国庆技术转让费20万元并赔偿利息损失。闫春梅不服提出上诉。江苏省高级人民法院二审认为涉案合同应为技术转让及合作经营合同，维持了一审判决。闫春梅不服二审判决，以涉案合同为合作经营合同、朱国庆未设立合同约定的公司等理由向最高人民法院申请再审。最高人民法院认定涉案合同的性质为预付前期技术转让费加利润提成方式的技术转让合同，并于2009年5月25日裁定驳回闫春梅的再审申请。

最高人民法院审查认为，判断本案合同性质的关键在于对合同第5条"公司的股份确认"的理解，对此应适用合同法第一百二十五条第一款的规定确定该条的真实意思。首先，从合同第5条使用的词句来看，不能当然得出必须设立以朱国庆、闫春梅、季新华为股东的公司的明确意思表示。其次，从合同第5条和有关条款来看，合同第5条所约定的"股份"并未明确就是有限责任公司股东的出资份额，而实际是指提取公司利润的计算标准。合同第5条在明确占有公司股份的权利时强调的是获得公司利润的比例，虽然也有承担公司风险的义务，但根据合同第6条的约定，闫春梅与公司资产无关，闫春梅实际上无法承担公司风险。在最高人民法院听证时闫春梅也认可，25%的股份实际上是指有权获得公司利润的25%。季新华是双方合同的中介人，天祥公司未将其列为股东，季新华也未对此提出异议，再次印证了所谓股份对闫春梅、季新华而言仅是指提取利润的比例。再次，从合同的目的来看，设立由朱国庆、闫春梅、季新华为股东的公司并非实现合同目的所必须。合同目的是指合同双方当事人通过合同的订立和履行，期望最终得到的东西、结果或者达到的状态。合同目的通常表现为一种经济利益。根据涉案合同的具体内容，闫春梅与朱国庆订立合同的目的在于通过技术转让获取利润。该目的的实现不以设立由朱国庆、闫春梅、季新华为股东的公司所必须。又次，从交易习惯来说，在技术转让交易中，存在以固定部分转让费（也叫预付入门费）加利润提成作为技术转让计费方式的习惯。最后，从诚实信用原则来看，在天祥公司成立后，闫春梅让其丈夫帮助天祥公司购买生产设备，并没有对天祥公司的成立不符合约定提出异议。综上，涉案合同应当属于预付前期技术转让费加利润提成方式的技术转让合同。合同中所约定的财务监督、技术指导等内容，表面上是合作经营内容，实际上是技术转让合同中技术转让方的附随义务。

28. 演艺经纪公司与演员签订的演艺合同及其中演出安排条款的性质及效力

随着演艺产业的蓬勃发展，近年来，演艺经纪公司与演员之间因演艺合同引发的纠纷逐渐增多。对于演艺经纪公司与演员签订的演艺合同及其中演出安排条款的性质及效力问题，实践中存在不同的理解。

在申请再审人熊威、杨洋与被申请人北京正合世纪文化传播有限公司（以下简称世纪公司）知识产权合同纠纷案〔（2009）民申字第1203号〕中，最高人民法院明确了演艺合同是一种综合性合同，关于演出安排的条款既非代理性质也非行纪性质，而是综合性合同中的一部分，不能依据合同法关于代理合同或行纪合同的规定孤立地对演出安排条款适用"单方解除"规则。

该案的基本案情是：2006年3月熊威、杨洋与世纪公司签订合同约定：世纪公司聘用熊威、杨洋为签约歌手，世纪公司全权代理熊威、杨洋唱片、演艺、广告事宜，如有违约，熊威、杨洋须按约定支付违约金；营利性演艺活动的收入由双方按约定比例分成；双方共同筹措资金，制作、发行、宣传唱片，版税由双方按比例分成；合同期内唱片的著作权归世纪公司；合同有效期为2006年3月23日至2009年3月22日等。合同签订后，熊威、杨洋参加了世纪公司安排的演出，为制作音乐专辑筹集了资金；世纪公司获取了音乐专集版税，向熊威、杨洋支付了一定的演出费。2007年1月12日，熊威、杨洋以世纪公司拖欠演出费及版税为由要求解除合同，世纪公司要求二人继续履行合同。熊威、杨洋遂诉至法院，请求判决确认合同关于演出安排的条款因违反《营业性演出管理条例》无效；如果有效，其可以依据合同法规定随时解除该部分条款等。北京市第二中级人民法院一审认定，本案合同中关于演出安排的约定属世纪公司与演员之间的代理行为，不属于《营业性演出管理条例》规范的营业性演出居间、代理、行纪活动，该合同不违反相关法律及行政法规的强制性规定，应确认有效；世纪公司的违约行为尚不致产生合同目的不能实现的后果，熊威、杨洋不能因此解除合同。世纪公司，熊威、杨洋均不服，提起上诉。北京市高级人民法院二审维持原判。熊威、杨洋仍不服，向最高人民法院申请再审。最高人民法院于2009年11月27日裁定驳回其再审申请。

最高人民法院审查认为，本案合同关于演出安排的条款不违反《营业性演出管理条例》的强制性规定，应确认为有效。本案合同不仅包含关于演出安排的约定，还包含世纪公司对熊威、杨洋商业运作、包装、推广以及著作权使用许可等多方面内容，而且各部分内容相互联系、相互依存，构成双方完整的权利义务关系。关于演出安排的条款既非代理性质也非行纪性质，而是本案综合性合同中的一部分。割裂该部分条款与合同其他部分的关系，孤立地对该部分条款适用"单方解除"规则，有违合同权利义务的一致性、均衡性及公平性。因此，熊威、杨洋关于其有权依据合同法关于代理合同或行纪合同的规定随时解除本案合同中演出安排条款的主张不能成立。

六、关于知识产权侵权责任承担

29. 专利侵权损害赔偿数额的确定

由于知识产权侵权损害的无形性、不确定性和因果关系的复杂性，侵权损害赔偿数额的确定在实际操作中比较困难和复杂，对有关赔偿确定因素的把握应重点考虑其合理性和成比例性。

In the case of Appellant Hua Jiping and Hefei Andihua Import and Export Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Andihua Company) v. Appellee Shanghai Sibotin Trading Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Sibotin Company), Rudong County Fengli Machinery Factory Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Fengli Company), and Nantong Tianlong Plastics Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Tianlong Company) — dispute over infringement of patent rights [ (2007) Min San Zhong Zi No. 3, hereinafter referred to as the "Suitcase" patent infringement case], where multiple factors such as the quantity of infringing products sold, the patent license fee, and the profit margin of infringing products coexisted, the Supreme People's Court conducted a specific and in-depth analysis of how to reasonably determine the amount of damages. The Supreme People's Court also held that in determining the amount of damages for intellectual property infringement, the degree of subjective fault of the parties may be considered in determining the corresponding liability for damages, especially when a specific calculation standard needs to be determined by discretion, the degree of subjective fault of the parties should be considered.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: Hua Jiping was the patentee of a utility model patent titled "Dumbbell Set Suitcase," with an authorization announcement date of December 10, 1999. Hua Jiping and an unrelated party invested and established Andihua Company on May 14, 2001, with Hua Jiping serving as the legal representative. On January 18, 2003, Hua Jiping granted Andihua Company a "non-exclusive and non-transferable license" for the patent in question, stipulating an annual license fee of RMB 5 million. On August 16, 2004, Hua Jiping transferred all his shares in Andihua Company to an unrelated party and ceased to serve as legal representative. In October 2005, Hua Jiping applied to Nantong Customs to seize 2,160 dumbbell set suitcases exported by Sibotin Company and Fengli Company, on the grounds that they infringed its patent rights. He then applied to the Jiangsu High People's Court for a pre-litigation order to cease patent infringement and for asset preservation. Subsequently, Hua Jiping and Andihua Company filed a lawsuit with the Jiangsu High People's Court. The Jiangsu High People's Court held at first instance that Sibotin Company and Fengli Company jointly infringed the patent rights of the two plaintiffs. Since the two plaintiffs provided the infringement quantity and the profit situation of the patented product from Sibotin Company and Fengli Company, the amount of damages should be determined based on the plaintiffs' losses in accordance with the law. Based on the value of the patented suitcase itself and its role in realizing the profit of the packaged dumbbell products, combined with factors such as the profit margins claimed by the parties, a reasonable profit margin of 15% of the selling price of the dumbbell products in question could be determined for the patented suitcase. The court then ordered Sibotin Company and Fengli Company to immediately cease infringement, destroy the seized dumbbell set suitcases, and jointly compensate the two plaintiffs for economic losses of RMB 682,129.56, as well as reasonable expenses of RMB 20,000 for stopping the infringement, attorney fees of RMB 110,000, and the actual storage costs incurred for the seized dumbbell set suitcases. Hua Jiping, Andihua Company, and Sibotin Company all appealed. The Supreme People's Court affirmed the original judgment and dismissed the appeals on June 11, 2009.

The Supreme People's Court held during the trial that when the quantity of infringing products sold can be determined, the loss of the infringed party or the benefit obtained by the infringer can be calculated based on the profit margin of the patented product or the infringing product, and the amount of damages can be determined accordingly. Where the profit margin of the relevant product is difficult to calculate accurately, the People's Court may determine a reasonable profit margin by discretion. Of course, if the parties can prove that there is a genuine and reasonable patent license fee calculated on a per-product basis, the damages may also be calculated by multiplying the per-unit fee by the quantity of infringing products. However, in this case, the so-called patent license fee was calculated on an annual basis, not on a per-product basis, and thus could not be used for reference. Furthermore, even if the method of referring to the patent license fee were adopted to calculate damages, the plaintiff must also bear the burden of proving the authenticity and reasonableness of the patent license fee. In this case, when the patent implementation license contract was signed, the patentee was a shareholder and legal representative of the licensee. There was clearly a conflict of interest between them. Although the patentee later transferred all his shares to another person and ceased to be the legal representative, this alone could not eliminate reasonable doubt about the authenticity and reasonableness of the patent license fee. Moreover, the plaintiff failed to provide evidence that the patent license fee had been actually paid and the corresponding taxes had been paid in accordance with the law. Therefore, the authenticity and reasonableness of the patent license fee should not be recognized in this case. All parties to this case objected to the reasonable profit margin of 15% determined by the lower court. The two plaintiffs argued that damages should be calculated based on a profit margin of 44% according to the cost accounting table they submitted on appeal. However, they had previously claimed a 30% profit margin in the first instance, and the evidence they now submitted did not constitute newly discovered evidence after the conclusion of the first instance trial and could not be admitted as new evidence in the appellate proceedings. Even if the evidence were admissible, since the relevant content was the result of the plaintiffs' own calculations, without other evidence to corroborate it, the authenticity of its content could not be recognized solely based on the stamp of the tax authority. Furthermore, even if the profit margin were genuine, it would only be the overall profit margin of the 20KG barbell set products exported using the patented packaging box in question, and it could not be taken for granted that the entire profit of the exported complete product set should be attributed to the patented packaging box itself. The two infringers' claim that the price of the patented packaging box should be calculated based on the price difference between products using the patented packaging box and products using paper packaging boxes, and that the profit margin should be determined accordingly, was reasonable to a certain extent but not absolutely accurate. Based on specific marketing strategies, the price difference between patented and non-patented products does not necessarily reflect the contribution of the patent. At the same time, in determining the amount of damages for intellectual property infringement, the degree of subjective fault of the parties may be considered in determining the corresponding liability for damages, especially when a specific calculation standard needs to be determined by discretion, the degree of subjective fault of the parties should be considered. In this case, after Sibotin Company terminated its procurement relationship with Andihua Company for dumbbell products using the patented suitcase in question, it proceeded to procure the same products from Fengli Company. This demonstrated obvious subjective fault, which should be reflected in the amount of damages. Taking all factors into consideration, the lower court, in a situation where the parties were unable to accurately prove the profit margins of the relevant patented product or infringing product, determined a reasonable profit margin of 15% of the selling price of the dumbbell products in question for the patented packaging box in question, based on the infringers' admitted profit margin for dumbbell products using the patented suitcase in question, combined with the profit margin of the right holder's own products claimed at the time, and also considering the value of the patented product and the infringing product themselves and the contribution of the packaging of the dumbbell products sold in the market to the overall product sales profit. Although relatively high, given the obvious subjective fault of the infringers, this discretionary profit margin was not clearly inappropriate and did not need to be changed.

30. Determination of the Amount of Reasonable Expenses for Investigating and Stopping the Infringement

In intellectual property infringement cases, right holders often claim compensation for reasonable expenses incurred in investigating and stopping the infringement. How to determine the scope and amount of such reasonable expenses directly relates to whether the right holder's enforcement costs can be reasonably compensated. The key is to consider the general situation of market enforcement.

In the aforementioned "Suitcase" patent infringement case, the Supreme People's Court also made specific analyses and determinations, based on the parties' allegations and defenses, regarding the determination of the amount of reasonable expenses for investigating and stopping the infringement and the nature of the guarantee provided by the right holder for the infringing goods when applying for customs measures.

The Supreme People's Court held that all expenses incurred by the right holder in investigating and stopping the infringement, as long as they are reasonable, can be included in the scope of compensation. Such reasonable expenses do not necessarily need to be evidenced one by one by receipts. The People's Court may, based on the specific circumstances of the case, consider other expenses that may indeed have been incurred, within the amount of reasonable expenses claimed by the plaintiff, and comprehensively determine the amount of reasonable expenses to be compensated. In this case, the expenses for traffic violation fines and the purchase of cigarettes and chewing gum incurred by the right holder during the investigation of the infringement were clearly unreasonable and should indeed be excluded. Meal expenses amounting to thousands of yuan were also unreasonable and should be given due consideration when comprehensively determining the amount of reasonable expenses. The purchase of general food and beverages constituted normal expenses necessary for maintaining ordinary bodily needs of the investigating personnel during their investigation activities and were not unreasonable expenses. Regarding accommodation and taxi expenses incurred at different hotels on the same day, the right holder's explanation that the investigation team conducted infringement investigations at multiple locations at the same time was reasonable and not clearly unreasonable. Among the so-called preliminary expenses of RMB 340,000 claimed by the plaintiff as reasonable expenses, the main components were the guarantee of RMB 240,000 for the infringing goods paid by the third party, Hefei Andi Fitness Products Co., Ltd., when Nantong Customs detained the infringing products in question, and the expenses incurred for the detained goods up to the conclusion of the enforcement of the judgment in this case. Pursuant to the relevant provisions of the Regulations of the People's Republic of China on Customs Protection of Intellectual Property Rights, the guarantee provided by the intellectual property right holder to Customs is used to compensate for losses that may be caused to the consignee or consignor due to improper application and to pay for the storage, custody, and disposal of goods detained by Customs. Where the goods suspected of infringement are determined to infringe intellectual property rights, the intellectual property right holder may include the relevant storage, custody, and disposal expenses it has paid as reasonable expenses incurred for stopping the infringement. Accordingly, when infringement of intellectual property rights is established, after deducting the storage, custody, and disposal expenses paid by the right holder for the goods detained by Customs, the guarantee will be returned to the right holder. Therefore, the guarantee cannot automatically be calculated as the parties' losses. Only the relevant expenses for storage, custody, and disposal of the infringing goods paid by the right holder can be included as reasonable expenses for stopping the infringement and be compensated.

31. Remuneration for Using Musical Works Adapted from Folk Songs

Regarding the standard of remuneration for using musical works adapted by others from folk songs, the Supreme People's Court, in the aforementioned "Dasheng Company Case," clarified the standard for using such works. The Supreme People's Court held that when a person uses a musical work adapted from a folk song to make a sound recording and reproduces or distributes it, full remuneration may be paid to the adapter.

In its ruling in this case, the Supreme People's Court pointed out that in the absence of an agreement between the parties, the standard of remuneration may be determined in accordance with the Interim Provisions on Remuneration Standards for Statutory Licensing of Sound Recordings issued by the National Copyright Administration. This case involved multiple users of musical works. Whose name is used to pay remuneration to the copyright owner should follow the agreement between the parties or industry practice. Since the law does not require that remuneration must be paid before the use of the work, the "use first, pay later" approach by the user does not violate the law, provided that the copyright owner's right to receive remuneration is not prejudiced. Folk songs generally have the characteristics of being passed down through generations without a specific author. The copyright owner of a musical work adapted from a folk song enjoys copyright in the adapted musical work in accordance with the law. When a person uses a musical work adapted from a folk song to make a sound recording and reproduces or distributes it, full remuneration may be paid to the adapter. In this case, the remuneration for the unpaid 700,000 copies of the musical work was calculated as: wholesale price of RMB 6.5 x royalty rate of 3.5% x distribution quantity of sound recordings of 700,000 copies / 11 tracks = RMB 14,477.

32. Civil Liability for Infringement of a Registered Trademark That Has Not Been Actually Used in Commerce

In a trademark infringement dispute, if the registered trademark sought to be protected has not been actually used in commerce, the trademark owner will generally have no actual loss when the registered trademark is infringed. In such a case, the manner in which the infringer bears liability for infringement has certain particularities.

In the aforementioned "Red River" trademark infringement case, the Supreme People's Court also clarified for the first time the issue of civil liability for infringement of a registered trademark that has not been actually used in commerce. The ruling in this case reflected the following judicial principle: where a registered trademark that has not been actually used in commerce is infringed, the infringer should bear the civil liability of ceasing the infringement and compensating the right holder for reasonable expenses incurred in stopping the infringement, but may not be ordered to bear civil liability for compensating losses. This judicial principle properly handles the relationship between the actual use of the registered trademark and the bearing of civil liability, making the assumption of civil liability conducive to encouraging trademark use and activating trademark resources, while also preventing trademark owners from using registered trademarks to seek improper benefits.

The Supreme People's Court held that the act of Yunnan Red River Company using the words "Red River Beer" on an advertising banner hanging in its sales department constituted, without permission, using the same text as the registered trademark as an unregistered trademark on the same goods, which was an act of infringing the exclusive right to use a registered trademark. For this infringement, Yunnan Red River Company should bear the civil liability of ceasing the infringement. The respondent did not submit evidence to prove that its "Red River" registered trademark had been actually used, nor did it prove that it had suffered actual losses due to the infringement. However, the respondent objectively would have incurred some losses in stopping the infringement. Considering the overall circumstances of the case, the discretionary amount of compensation to be paid by the applicant for retrial to the two respondents for their losses was determined to be a total of RMB 20,000.

33. Liability for Ceasing Use When the Sued Business Name Constitutes Unfair Competition

According to Article 4 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Civil Disputes over Conflicts between Registered Trademarks, Business Names, and Prior Rights, where the sued business name constitutes unfair competition, the People's Court may, based on the plaintiff's claims and the specific circumstances of the case, order the defendant to bear civil liability such as ceasing use, standardized use, etc.

In the case of the applicant for retrial, Guangdong Xingqun Food and Beverage Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xingqun Food and Beverage Company), and the respondents, Guangzhou Xingqun (Pharmaceutical) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xingqun Pharmaceutical Company) and Guangzhou Xingqun (Pharmaceutical) Co., Ltd. Nutritional Supplement Factory (hereinafter referred to as Xingqun Nutritional Supplement Factory) — dispute over unfair competition [ (2008) Min Shen Zi No. 982], the Supreme People's Court further clarified that if ceasing use of the business name is necessary to prevent market confusion, the defendant may be ordered to cease use. The Supreme People's Court pointed out that where a party maliciously uses a trade name from the business name of another party that has a certain market reputation and is known to the relevant public, and due to being in the same geographical area, it is highly likely to cause confusion among the relevant public, the People's Court may directly order that party to bear civil liability for ceasing use of its business name.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: Xingqun Pharmaceutical Company began using "Xingqun" as its trade name in 1950. Although there was a period of interrupted use after 1966, it has continuously used the trade name since 1980. After years of operation, Xingqun Pharmaceutical Company's trademarks "Qunxing" and "Qunxing + Device" were repeatedly recognized as well-known trademarks since 1992. Its Xia Sang Ju product received provincial and national awards for quality products or famous brand products multiple times since 1985. Xingqun Pharmaceutical Company received numerous corporate honors since 1986 and was recognized by the Ministry of Commerce as one of the first batch of China Time-honored Brands on November 7, 2006. The "Xia Sang Ju Granules" produced by Xingqun Pharmaceutical Company sold well and had extensive domestic and overseas markets. Xingqun Pharmaceutical Company placed a large number of advertisements for "Xia Sang Ju Granules" in various media. On January 14, 2005, Xingqun Food and Beverage Company was registered and established with the Guangdong Provincial Administration for Industry and Commerce. The "Xia Sang Ju Granules" produced by this company were similar in packaging and decoration to those of Xingqun Pharmaceutical Company. Xingqun Pharmaceutical Company and Xingqun Nutritional Supplement Factory filed a lawsuit on October 25, 2006, requesting the court to find that the trade name used by Xingqun Food and Beverage Company infringed its right to a business name and constituted unfair competition, and requesting that Xingqun Food and Beverage Company be ordered to cease using "Xingqun" as its trade name and compensate for economic losses. The Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court held at first instance that Xingqun Food and Beverage Company's use of its business name did not infringe the business name rights of Xingqun Pharmaceutical Company and Xingqun Nutritional Supplement Factory, and dismissed all claims of the two plaintiffs. After the two plaintiffs appealed, the Guangdong High People's Court held at second instance that the conduct of Xingqun Food and Beverage Company constituted unfair competition. It modified the judgment, ordering Xingqun Food and Beverage Company to cease using the trade name "Xingqun" in its business name, apply to the Guangdong Provincial Administration for Industry and Commerce to change the trade name "Xingqun" in its business name, and compensate for losses. Xingqun Food and Beverage Company refused to accept the judgment and applied for retrial to the Supreme People's Court. The Supreme People's Court ruled on September 24, 2009 to dismiss its application for retrial.

The Supreme People's Court held upon review that if a business operator subsequently chooses to use a trade name that is already known to the relevant public and has a certain market reputation as its own trade name, produces products similar to those of others, and uses similar decoration, and due to being in the same geographical area, it is likely to cause confusion, it should be considered to have obvious malice of "free-riding." The People's Court may directly order that business operator to bear civil liability for ceasing use of its business name in a civil judgment. Although the administration of business names falls within the purview of industrial and commercial administrative authorities, the use of a business name that infringes upon the lawful civil rights and interests of others, constituting infringement or unfair competition, falls within the purview of judicial power of the People's Court, and the People's Court has the authority to apply civil liability methods to deal with the corresponding civil infringement or unfair competition.

34. Reasonable Sharing of Case Acceptance Fees

In the aforementioned "Suitcase" patent infringement case, regarding the burden of the case acceptance fee, Sibotin Company pointed out in its appeal that it should be determined in proportion to the amount claimed by the plaintiff and the amount supported by the court. In response, the Supreme People's Court clarified the factors to be considered in the sharing of case acceptance fees in this case.

The Supreme People's Court held that whether under the former Measures for Litigation Fee Collection of the People's Courts or the current Measures for the Payment of Litigation Fees, the principle for the burden of litigation fees is the same, i.e., the losing party bears the fee. Where a party prevails in part and loses in part, the People's Court shall determine the respective amounts to be borne by the parties based on the specific circumstances of the case. Especially in infringement cases, the sharing of the case acceptance fee should not only consider the proportion of the plaintiff's claimed amount that is supported, but also, more importantly, consider whether the infringement alleged by the plaintiff is itself established. Additionally, the degree to which the plaintiff's other claims are supported and the specific circumstances of the parties' exercise of their litigation rights, such as whether there is obvious fault, may also be considered. It should not be determined solely based on the proportion of the amount claimed by the plaintiff to the amount supported by the court.

VII. Evidence in Intellectual Property Litigation

35. Evidentiary Qualification and Examination of Certification of Copyright Ownership Issued by Institutions Without Copyright Certification Authority

In copyright infringement cases involving foreign works, parties often use certifications of copyright ownership issued by permanent institutions established in China by foreign copyright certification bodies as evidence to prove their rights in the foreign work. The courts have divergent views on the probative force of such evidence.

In the case of the petitioner for retrial, Guangdong Zhongkai Cultural Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhongkai Company), v. the respondent, Shijiazhuang Zhanshen Legend Internet Cafe (hereinafter referred to as Zhanshen Internet Cafe), concerning a copyright infringement dispute [Case No. (2009) Min Shen Zi No. 127], the Supreme People's Court held that the Beijing Representative Office of the Korean Copyright Commission for Deliberation and Mediation could only engage in liaison activities related to copyright authentication, but did not have the qualifications to certify copyright ownership; the determination of ownership of copyright in overseas works should be made by comprehensively evaluating other evidence, such as lawfully published publications.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: Zhongkai Company filed a lawsuit alleging that Korean MBC Company was the copyright owner of the television series "Goong S," and that Korean MBC Company had authorized Zhongkai Company to exclusively hold the relevant rights, including the right to communicate the work via information networks in Mainland China. It claimed that Zhanshen Internet Cafe, without permission, placed the work on the internet cafe's server for public download and viewing, thereby infringing upon its lawful rights and interests. Zhongkai Company submitted a certificate issued by the Beijing Representative Office of the Korean Copyright Commission for Deliberation and Mediation as evidence to prove that Korean MBC Company owned the copyright in the television series "Goong S." The Shijiazhuang Intermediate People's Court of Hebei Province held at the first instance that the certificate issued by the Beijing Representative Office of the Korean Copyright Commission for Deliberation and Mediation lacked probative force and could not prove that MBC Company owned the copyright in "Goong S," and accordingly dismissed Zhongkai Company's lawsuit. After an appeal, the Hebei High People's Court upheld the first-instance ruling on the same grounds at the second instance. Zhongkai Company, still dissatisfied, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. On May 19, 2009, the Supreme People's Court issued a ruling instructing the Hebei High People's Court to conduct a retrial.

The Supreme People's Court held in its review that, in accordance with the "Measures for the Administration of Overseas Copyright Authentication Agencies Establishing Permanent Offices in China," the Beijing Representative Office of the Korean Copyright Commission for Deliberation and Mediation could only engage in liaison activities related to copyright authentication and did not have the qualifications to certify the ownership of copyright in overseas works. However, with respect to the ownership of the copyright in the film and television work "Goong S" involved in the case, the certificate issued by the Beijing Representative Office of the Korean Copyright Commission for Deliberation and Mediation was only one piece of evidence provided by Zhongkai Company. In addition to assessing the probative force of this evidence, the court should also have made a comprehensive determination by considering other evidence, such as lawfully published audio-visual products, the approval form for imported audio-visual products, and the certificate of rights and interests submitted by Zhongkai Company. The original trial ruling failed to conduct cross-examination or authentication of the above evidence and simply dismissed Zhongkai Company's lawsuit on the sole ground that the certificate issued by the Beijing Representative Office of the Korean Copyright Commission for Deliberation and Mediation lacked probative force, which was improper.

36. Examination and determination of the rights holder and the facts of the act in cases of infringement of the rights of producers of sound recordings

In cases of disputes over infringement of the rights of producers of audio-visual recordings, due to the composite nature of right holders on audio-visual products and the complexity of infringing acts, it is difficult for producers of audio-visual products to prove the establishment of the infringing act.

In the case of the petitioner for retrial, Maoming (Shuidong) Jiahe Technology Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jiahe Company), v. the respondent, Beijing Tianzhong Culture Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Tianzhong Culture Company), and the defendants at the first instance, Zibo Jindi Shopping Plaza Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jindi Shopping Plaza) and Liaoning Radio and Television Audio-visual Publishing House (hereinafter referred to as Liaoning Audio-visual Publishing House), concerning a dispute over infringement of neighboring rights [Case No. (2008) Min Shen Zi No. 453], the Supreme People's Court clarified the issues of examination and determination of the right holder and the facts of the act in such cases.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: Tianzhong Culture Company lawfully enjoyed the rights of a producer of sound recordings in relation to nine tracks involved in the CD "Sun Yue - Lily Flower," which it produced, distributed, and performed by Sun Yue. On April 27, 2006, Tianzhong Culture Company purchased a box of allegedly infringing optical discs at Jindi Shopping Plaza, which issued a sales invoice stating "VCD optical discs." The color-printed outer packaging of the optical discs bore the label "Red Card Appearance, Three Stars Shining," with the fourth disc core labeled "Sun Yue B." The disc seal listed the titles of songs performed by Sun Yue, including the above nine tracks for which Tianzhong Culture Company claimed rights. According to the source identification code (SID code) and the publication registration number displayed on the optical discs, the units that replicated and distributed the optical discs were Jiahe Technology Company and Liaoning Audio-visual Publishing House, respectively. Tianzhong Culture Company filed a lawsuit with the court, alleging that Jiahe Technology Company and Liaoning Audio-visual Publishing House had infringed upon its rights of reproduction and distribution, and requested that the defendants be ordered to cease sales and compensate for economic losses. The Zibo Intermediate People's Court of Shandong Province found at the first instance that Tianzhong Culture Company enjoyed the rights of a producer of sound recordings in the above nine tracks involved in the case. The sales invoice from Jindi Shopping Plaza, which stated "VCD optical discs," was sufficient to prove that the allegedly infringing optical discs were purchased from Jindi Shopping Plaza. Although the allegedly infringing optical discs were VCD products and Tianzhong Culture Company's rights were over CD tracks, the same audio source could be converted between different formats. The nine tracks involved in the allegedly infringing VCD in the case were all indicated as performed by Sun Yue, which was identical to the original performance of the tracks for which Tianzhong Culture Company claimed rights. Jiahe Technology Company and Liaoning Audio-visual Publishing House failed to provide relevant evidence to prove a lawful source for the songs they replicated. Therefore, it should be determined that the nine tracks in the allegedly infringing optical discs originated from the same audio source as the identical tracks in Tianzhong Culture Company's CD album "Sun Yue - Lily Flower." The allegedly infringing optical discs bore the words "published by Liaoning Audio-visual Publishing House," and the SID code "ifpiv103" displayed on them belonged to Jiahe Technology Company. Liaoning Audio-visual Publishing House failed to provide evidence proving it had obtained lawful authorization, and Jiahe Technology Company also failed to provide evidence proving that the replication of the allegedly infringing optical discs was done by another party or that there were grounds for exoneration. The three defendants had infringed upon Tianzhong Culture Company's rights as a producer of sound recordings. The court then ordered Jiahe Technology Company and Liaoning Audio-visual Publishing House to jointly compensate Tianzhong Culture Company for economic losses of RMB 225,000. After Jiahe Technology Company appealed, the Shandong High People's Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the original judgment at the second instance. Jiahe Technology Company, still dissatisfied, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. On May 19, 2009, the Supreme People's Court issued a ruling dismissing its application for retrial.

The Supreme People's Court held in its review that, with respect to the issue of proving whether Tianzhong Culture Company enjoyed the rights of a producer of sound recordings in the tracks involved in the case, Tianzhong Culture Company, in order to prove it enjoyed such rights, not only submitted two "Cooperation Agreements" signed with Yuezhi Sheng Company and a guarantee certificate from the performer Sun Yue, but also provided the lawfully published album "Sun Yue - Lily Flower." Based on the above agreements, the guarantee certificate, and the copyright management information displayed on the lawfully published product, it could be determined that Tianzhong Culture Company lawfully enjoyed the rights of a producer of sound recordings in the nine tracks performed by Sun Yue involved in the case. Whether Tianzhong Culture Company held an "Audio-visual Product Production License" did not affect Tianzhong Culture Company's right to exercise its claim. Regarding the issue of the correspondence between the sales invoice and the allegedly infringing optical discs, Tianzhong Culture Company provided the allegedly infringing optical discs it had purchased and the sales invoice issued by Jindi Shopping Plaza. Whether the sales invoice could serve as evidence for Tianzhong Culture Company to claim its rights should be examined based on the relevant case facts. Jindi Shopping Plaza did not dispute the authenticity of the sales invoice it had issued, but claimed that there was no correspondence between the sales invoice and the allegedly infringing optical discs. The burden of proof on this issue should be borne by Jindi Shopping Plaza. Regarding the issue of whether Jiahe Technology Company should bear liability for infringement, based on the copyright management information on the allegedly infringing optical discs, it could be determined that the optical discs were published and distributed by Liaoning Audio-visual Publishing House and replicated by Jiahe Technology Company. At the original trial, Jiahe Technology Company and Liaoning Audio-visual Publishing House only raised the defense that the nine tracks performed by Sun Yue in the allegedly infringing optical discs they replicated and distributed were downloaded from the internet and were not copied from the sound recordings produced by Tianzhong Culture Company, but they failed to provide relevant evidence to prove this. This defense could not be established.

37. Examination and determination of the authenticity of evidence after a party abandons the application for expert evaluation

When a party disputes the authenticity of a piece of evidence and once applies for expert evaluation, but the application is deemed withdrawn due to reasons such as failure to pay the evaluation fees as required, there may be confusion in practice regarding how the people's court should examine and determine such evidence and whether it can directly deny or affirm the authenticity of the evidence solely on the ground that the party abandoned the application for expert evaluation.

In the case of the petitioner for retrial, Shenzhen Shuoxing Transportation Electronic Equipment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Shuoxing Company), v. the respondent, Yuhuan Longzhong Motorcycle Parts Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Longzhong Company), concerning a dispute over a patent licensing and technical service contract [Case No. (2009) Min Shen Zi No. 1325], the Supreme People's Court held that, in the absence of judicial expert evaluation of the evidence, a comprehensive determination of its authenticity should still be made based on the source, formation circumstances, objective condition, and other evidence in the case. The authenticity of the evidence cannot be directly denied on the sole ground that the party abandoned the application for expert evaluation.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: On July 21, 2006, Shuoxing Company and Longzhong Company entered into a "Patent License and Technical Cooperation Contract," under which Shuoxing Company licensed to Longzhong Company the use of three patented technologies, including the motor winding and forming stator, and guaranteed to assist Longzhong Company in producing products meeting the acceptance standards within the specified period. After the contract was signed, Longzhong Company paid the first and second installments of fees amounting to RMB 100,000. Shuoxing Company provided technical documents and technical guidance to Longzhong Company, which used the three patented technologies provided by Shuoxing Company for production. During the product trial production phase, Longzhong Company commissioned Lida Precision Mould (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Lida Mould Company) to make and modify molds. As of the time of the lawsuit at the first instance, the parties had not conducted acceptance testing or issued a written acceptance certificate as stipulated in Article 6 of the contract. Shuoxing Company filed a lawsuit with the court because it had not received the third installment of patent usage fees, requesting that the defendant pay the third installment of patent usage fees, mold fees, and mold modification fees. One of the main bases for Shuoxing Company to prove its claims was the work notebook of Shen Huaisheng, a former employee of Longzhong Company, and Shuoxing Company had once applied to the court of first instance for expert evaluation of the notebook's authenticity. The Taizhou Intermediate People's Court of Zhejiang Province held at the first instance that, although Shuoxing Company had applied for expert evaluation of the notebook, its refusal to pay the evaluation fees was deemed as abandoning the application for expert evaluation. Moreover, Shen Huaisheng himself did not appear in court as a witness, and the source of the work notebook was unclear. Therefore, the authenticity of the contents recorded in the notebook could not be determined. The court then dismissed Shuoxing Company's claims. Shuoxing Company, dissatisfied, appealed. The Zhejiang High People's Court at the second instance held that Shuoxing Company had failed to pre-pay the evaluation fees, and the court of first instance's decision to withdraw the commission for expert evaluation of Shen Huaisheng's notebook was appropriate. The authenticity of the notebook could not be recognized, and Shuoxing Company's claims lacked sufficient evidence. The court dismissed the appeal. Shuoxing Company applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. During the retrial review, the Supreme People's Court, after comprehensively evaluating the evidence from various aspects, recognized the authenticity of Shen Huaisheng's work notebook and determined that the molds currently used by Longzhong Company belonged to Shuoxing Company. However, it also found that Longzhong Company, using Shuoxing Company's technology and under its guidance, had failed to produce qualified products meeting customer demand standards. Therefore, the condition for Shuoxing Company to require Longzhong Company to pay the third installment of patent licensing fees had not been satisfied. Accordingly, on December 28, 2009, the Supreme People's Court issued a ruling dismissing Shuoxing Company's application for retrial.

The Supreme People's Court held in its review that Shen Huaisheng's work notebook recorded the production activities of Longzhong Company from July 13, 2006, to January 23, 2007. The entries on consecutive pages of the notebook were coherent in terms of time and content, with no apparent interruption or discontinuity, and the times and work items recorded in it corresponded with other evidence submitted by Shuoxing Company. Additionally, both Shuoxing Company and Longzhong Company acknowledged that Shen Huaisheng had been an employee of Longzhong Company. Shuoxing Company produced the original work notebook at the retrial review hearing, and Longzhong Company failed to provide evidence proving that the notebook was forged. Based on this, the authenticity of the notebook and the contents recorded therein could be recognized.

VIII. Procedural Issues in Intellectual Property Litigation

38. Determination of Duplicate Lawsuits

Duplicate lawsuits not only impose additional burdens on the parties but also waste judicial resources. The prohibition of duplicate lawsuits is an inherent requirement of the principle of "res judicata" in civil litigation. How to identify duplicate lawsuits is one of the issues frequently encountered in judicial practice.

In the appeal case concerning the ruling on the false publicity dispute between Appellant Beijing Golden Holiday Travel Agency Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Golden Holiday Company) and Respondents Ctrip Computer Technology (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Ctrip Computer Company), Shanghai Ctrip Business Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Ctrip Business Company), Hebei Kanghui International Aviation Service Co., Ltd., and Beijing Ctrip International Travel Agency Co., Ltd. [Case No. (2007) Min San Zhong Zi No. 4, referred to as the "Ctrip" Ruling Case], the Supreme People's Court clarified the criteria for identifying duplicate lawsuits, i.e., the key to determining whether a lawsuit is duplicative is whether it involves the same parties, based on the same legal relationship and same legal facts, seeking the same claims. In its ruling in this case, the Supreme People's Court also clarified that the continued implementation of conduct already adjudicated by a prior effective judgment still falls within the scope of res judicata of the effective judgment.

The basic facts of the case are as follows: Golden Holiday Company had previously filed a lawsuit against Ctrip Computer Company with the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court on the grounds of unfair competition. After the second instance, the Shanghai High People's Court rendered a civil judgment [Case No. (2005) Hu Gao Min San (Zhi) Zhong Zi No. 36, hereinafter referred to as Case No. 36]. This judgment held that Ctrip Computer Company's statement that "Ctrip Travel Network (Stock Code: CTRP) is the first Chinese tourism company listed on the NASDAQ in the United States" could not be deemed false because there was supporting evidence. It also found that the first-instance judgment's determination that whether a company exceeded its business scope to engage in illegal operations (Ctrip Computer Company was accused of illegally engaging in Internet information services business) did not fall within the scope of civil litigation accepted by the people's court was not inappropriate. Ctrip Computer Company had also filed a lawsuit against Golden Holiday Company for false publicity and business disparagement with the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court. Golden Holiday Company filed a counterclaim. The court consolidated the cases and rendered a first-instance judgment. This judgment found that Ctrip Computer Company's use of the absolute term "largest" in its publicity inherently implied exclusion of competitors and constituted an unfair competition act of engaging in misleading false publicity regarding its services. After the appeal, the Shanghai High People's Court, after trial, issued a civil judgment [Case No. (2006) Hu Gao Min San (Zhi) Zhong Zi No. 41], upholding the first-instance judgment. In the present case, which occurred after the above two cases, Golden Holiday Company, from July to September 2006, filed a lawsuit and then added defendants and additional claims, alleging that Ctrip Computer Company and three other companies constituted unfair competition. Some of its claims were as follows: seeking an order that Ctrip Computer Company and Ctrip Business Company cease the false publicity regarding "Ctrip Travel Network successfully listed on NASDAQ in the United States on December 9, 2003," "the first tourism company listed in the United States," and "Ctrip has the largest unified airline ticket booking system in the industry," and that Ctrip Computer Company cease its various business activities conducted through "Ctrip Travel Network (www.ctrip.com)" (on the grounds that, as a wholly foreign-owned enterprise, it had not obtained the relevant administrative licenses and could not operate value-added telecommunications services for Internet information services). The Hebei High People's Court at first instance held that the above claims in this case constituted duplicate lawsuits and accordingly issued a ruling [Case No. (2006) Ji Min San Chu Zi No. 3-1] dismissing Golden Holiday Company's lawsuit regarding the part of the case under trial. After Golden Holiday Company appealed, the Supreme People's Court, on October 22, 2009, issued a ruling dismissing the appeal and upholding the original ruling.

The Supreme People's Court held in its trial that the key to determining whether a lawsuit is duplicative is whether it involves the same parties, based on the same legal relationship and same legal facts, seeking the same claims. Although there were three additional defendant companies in this case, the plaintiff's claims were only directed against Ctrip Computer Company and Ctrip Business Company. The direct actor for the publicity at issue in this case was Ctrip Computer Company, and the entity ultimately liable was still Ctrip Computer Company. The plaintiff's claims were all seeking to stop publicity acts with substantially the same content. Although the timing and location of the alleged acts in the two cases were different, the continued implementation of conduct after the effective judgment that had already been determined to be lawful by a prior effective judgment still fell within the scope of res judicata of the effective judgment and should be protected by law and could not be sued again.

39. Jurisdiction Over Illegal Business Operations

With respect to whether a people's court can directly make a determination and handle a matter when, in civil litigation, a party claims that certain conduct violates relevant administrative laws and regulations, thus constituting an illegal business operation, and requests the court to order cessation of such illegal business operations, this directly involves the issue of the scope of cases accepted by the people's court and the jurisdiction over the case.

In the above-mentioned "Ctrip" Ruling Case, the Supreme People's Court held that whether Ctrip Computer Company's conduct constituted an illegal operation of value-added telecommunications services was a matter of whether it violated relevant administrative laws and regulations and should bear corresponding administrative liability. Such a matter should be investigated and determined by the competent administrative departments in accordance with the law and did not fall within the scope of examination in civil litigation by the people's court. In fact, Golden Holiday Company had previously filed a complaint with the relevant competent authorities regarding Ctrip Computer Company's alleged illegal engagement in Internet information services business, but as of that time, the relevant authorities had not yet made a clear determination of illegal operation or imposed penalties. Under these circumstances, the people's court was even less justified in making an examination and determination in civil litigation. The reasoning of the relevant determination in the previous Case No. 36 and the handling of the relevant claims by the court of first instance in the present case were not improper. There was no legal basis for Golden Holiday Company's request that the people's court independently examine the legality of the conduct at issue in civil litigation.

40. Jurisdiction Over Trade Secret Infringement Cases Based on Confidentiality or Non-competition Clauses in Labor Contracts

Article 79 of the Labor Law stipulates the pre-arbitration procedure for labor disputes. Only if a party is dissatisfied with the arbitration award may it file a lawsuit with the people's court. If an employer brings a trade secret infringement dispute based on confidentiality or non-competition clauses in a labor contract, the question arises as to whether the dispute should be resolved through the labor dispute handling procedure or can be directly accepted by the people's court as an unfair competition dispute.

In the case of Appellant Chen Jianxin v. Appellees Nantong Synthetic Materials Factory under the Ministry of Chemical Industry (hereinafter referred to as Synthetic Factory), Nantong Xingchen Synthetic Materials Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xingchen Company), Nantong Zhonglan Engineering Plastics Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhonglan Company), and the Defendants at First Instance Nantong Dongfang Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Dongfang Company), Zhou Chuanmin, Chen Xi, Li Daomin, and Dai Jianxun — dispute over jurisdiction objection for infringement of technical secrets and trade secrets [ (2008) Min San Zhong Zi No. 9 ], the Supreme People's Court clearly stated that, for disputes arising from non-competition agreements between employees and employers, if a party claims rights based on breach of contract, the dispute falls within the scope of labor disputes and shall be resolved through the labor dispute resolution procedures according to law; if a party claims rights based on infringement of trade secrets, the dispute falls within the scope of unfair competition disputes, and a people's court may directly accept such case according to law.

The basic facts of said case are as follows: The labor contracts and the Confidentiality and Non-Competition Agreement entered into between Synthetic Factory and Chen Jianxin and others from 2001 to 2004 all stipulated that any dispute between the parties could be submitted to the labor arbitration committee at the location of Synthetic Factory for arbitration. Dongfang Company was established on October 21, 2003, in which Zhou Chuanmin's father held shares, Zhou Chuanmin served as general manager, and Dai Jianxun and Chen Xi worked for the company. On March 17, 2008, Synthetic Factory, Xingchen Company, and Zhonglan Company filed a lawsuit with the Jiangsu High People's Court against Dongfang Company, Zhou Chuanmin, Chen Jianxin, Chen Xi, Li Daomin, and Dai Jianxun on the grounds that the six defendants had infringed upon their technical secrets and trade secrets. They alleged that the three plaintiffs, as affiliated enterprises, jointly engaged in the research, development, and production of plastics and related products, and owned the trade secrets involved in the case. They claimed that the six defendants jointly infringed on their trade secrets and requested the court to order each defendant to immediately cease the infringement and jointly and severally compensate the plaintiffs RMB 45 million. Defendant Chen Jianxin raised an objection to jurisdiction within the response period, primarily on the ground that the case was a labor dispute and should be decided by the Nantong Labor Arbitration Committee. The Jiangsu High People's Court held at first instance that the essence of the dispute was whether the plaintiffs lawfully owned the alleged trade secrets, whether the infringement was established, and the civil liability for infringement, rather than a dispute over rights and obligations arising from the employment relationship between the employer and employees. Therefore, the case was not a labor dispute and there was no issue of mandatory prior labor arbitration. The court ruled to dismiss the jurisdiction objection. Chen Jianxin, dissatisfied, appealed to the Supreme People's Court. The Supreme People's Court ruled on August 27, 2009, to dismiss the appeal and affirm the original ruling.

The Supreme People's Court held in its reasoning that Article 122 of the Contract Law provides that where a party's breach of contract infringes upon the personal or property rights of the other party, the injured party is entitled to choose, in accordance with this Law, to demand the breaching party bear liability for breach of contract, or, in accordance with other laws, to demand the breaching party bear tort liability. Accordingly, for disputes arising from contracts, when there is a concurrence of liability for breach of contract and tort liability, the plaintiff has the right to choose whether to file a contract action or a tort action, and the people's court shall determine whether to accept the case and determine the jurisdiction based on the cause of action raised by the plaintiff. Labor disputes are disputes between employees and employers arising from the legal relationship of a labor contract. Chinese law does not specifically require that parties to a labor contract may only file a labor dispute based on the labor contract. If an act violating a labor contract also constitutes a tort, the law does not preclude the injured party from requesting the tortfeasor to bear tort liability for the tortious act. Therefore, for disputes arising from non-competition agreements between employees and employers, if a party claims rights based on breach of contract, the dispute falls within the scope of labor disputes and shall be resolved through the labor dispute resolution procedures according to law; if a party claims rights based on infringement of trade secrets, the dispute falls within the scope of unfair competition disputes, and a people's court may directly accept such case according to law. In this case, the plaintiff Synthetic Factory had labor contract relationships with each individual defendant and had signed the Confidentiality and Non-Competition Agreement, which also contained an arbitration clause. However, the cause of action of this case was a dispute over infringement of technical secrets and trade secrets. The plaintiffs' claims were to request each individual defendant and defendant Dongfang Company to bear tort civil liability for ceasing the infringement of their trade secrets and compensating for losses. The subject matter of this case was the tort legal relationship between the plaintiffs and each defendant, not the labor contract legal relationship between the plaintiffs and each individual. Therefore, this case is not a labor dispute. As a tort case, a people's court may directly accept it.
